name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_STATEMENT_BASED_2_Q01 - Velocity and particle paths in rigid body motion

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In pure translational motion of a rigid body, every particle of the body moves with the same velocity at any given instant of time.

Statement II: In rotation of a rigid body about a fixed axis, all constituent particles describe circular paths whose planes are parallel to the axis of rotation.

In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle of Rigid Body Motion
A rigid body is defined as an extended system of particles where relative distances between all constituent particles remain constant. In pure translation, the orientation of any line segment within the body remains unchanged in space. In rotation about a fixed axis, every particle of the body moves in a circular path about the axis.

Step 2: Analysis of Statement I
During pure translational motion, every constituent particle undergoes identical displacement in any given time interval. Consequently, all particles have identical velocities and accelerations at any instant of time. Therefore, Statement I is scientifically correct.

Step 3: Analysis of Statement II
When a rigid body rotates about a fixed axis, each particle (not located on the axis itself) describes a circle whose centre lies on the rotation axis. The plane of each circle is perpendicular to the fixed axis of rotation, not parallel to it. Therefore, Statement II is scientifically incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Statement I is correct and Statement II is incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct and Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_STATEMENT_BASED_2_Q02 - Position of centre of mass in particle systems

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For a two-particle system composed of two particles of identical mass, the centre of mass lies exactly midway along the line joining them.

Statement II: If the origin of the coordinate system is chosen at the centre of mass of a system of particles, the sum of the mass moments \(\sum m_i \mathbf{r}_i\) is zero.

In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of Centre of Mass
The position vector of the centre of mass \(\mathbf{R}\) of a system of \(n\) particles having masses \(m_i\) and position vectors \(\mathbf{r}_i\) is defined as \(\mathbf{R} = \frac{\sum m_i \mathbf{r}_i}{\sum m_i}\).

Step 2: Analysis of Statement I
For a system consisting of two particles of equal mass \(m_1 = m_2 = m\) located at positions \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) along a line, the centre of mass coordinate is \(X = \frac{m x_1 + m x_2}{m + m} = \frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}\). This coordinate is the exact midpoint of the line segment joining the two particles. Therefore, Statement I is scientifically correct.

Step 3: Analysis of Statement II
When the origin is located at the centre of mass, the centre of mass position vector is null, \(\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{0}\). Substituting this into the definition gives \(\frac{\sum m_i \mathbf{r}_i}{M} = \mathbf{0}\), which directly leads to \(\sum m_i \mathbf{r}_i = \mathbf{0}\). Thus, the sum of mass moments about the centre of mass is zero. Therefore, Statement II is scientifically correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct and Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_STATEMENT_BASED_2_Q03 - Influence of internal forces on centre of mass

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The acceleration of the centre of mass of a system of particles is determined exclusively by the net external force acting on the system.

Statement II: Internal forces between constituent particles in an isolated system can alter the total linear momentum of the system of particles.

In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Newton's Second Law for a System of Particles
The total linear momentum \(\mathbf{P}\) of a system of particles is related to the motion of its centre of mass by \(\mathbf{P} = M \mathbf{V}_{cm}\). Differentiating with respect to time yields \(M \mathbf{A}_{cm} = \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{P}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \sum \mathbf{F}_{ext} + \sum \mathbf{F}_{int}\).

Step 2: Analysis of Statement I
By Newton's third law, mutual internal forces between any pair of particles within the system are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. Because they act along the line joining the interacting particles, the vector sum of all internal forces is identically zero (\(\sum \mathbf{F}_{int} = \mathbf{0}\)). Hence, \(M \mathbf{A}_{cm} = \mathbf{F}_{ext}\), proving that the acceleration of the centre of mass is determined solely by external forces. Therefore, Statement I is scientifically correct.

Step 3: Analysis of Statement II
Since all internal forces sum vectorially to zero, internal interactions cannot generate a net force on the system. Consequently, internal forces cannot change the total linear momentum \(\mathbf{P}\) of the system of particles. Therefore, Statement II is scientifically incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Statement I is correct and Statement II is incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct and Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_STATEMENT_BASED_2_Q04 - Commutativity and spatial reflection of vector products

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The vector product of two non-zero vectors is commutative, satisfying the relation \(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a}\).

Statement II: Under spatial reflection of coordinates through the origin where every polar vector changes sign, the cross product of two polar vectors does not invert sign.

In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition and Direction of Vector Product
The vector product of two vectors \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) is defined as \(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = (a b \sin\theta) \hat{\mathbf{n}}\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between them and \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) is a unit vector perpendicular to both, governed by the right-hand screw rule.

Step 2: Analysis of Statement I
Reversing the order of vectors in the right-hand rule reverses the direction of the resulting normal vector. Thus, \(\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a} = -(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})\). The vector product is strictly anticommutative, not commutative. Therefore, Statement I is scientifically incorrect.

Step 3: Analysis of Statement II
Under a spatial reflection (parity inversion), true polar vectors invert sign: \(\mathbf{a} \to -\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b} \to -\mathbf{b}\). The vector product transforms as \((-\mathbf{a}) \times (-\mathbf{b}) = \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}\), retaining its positive sign. The cross product of two polar vectors is an axial vector (pseudovector) that does not change sign under coordinate inversion. Therefore, Statement II is scientifically correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct and Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_STATEMENT_BASED_2_Q05 - External torque and conservation of angular momentum

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The time rate of change of the total angular momentum of a system of particles about a chosen point equals the net external torque acting on the system about that same point.

Statement II: If the net external torque acting on a system of particles about a given axis is zero, the component of angular momentum along that axis is conserved.

In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Rotational Analogue of Newton's Second Law
For a system of particles, the total angular momentum \(\mathbf{L}\) about a fixed origin or the centre of mass satisfies the relation \(\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{L}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \boldsymbol{\tau}_{ext}\), where \(\boldsymbol{\tau}_{ext}\) represents the net external torque about the identical reference point.

Step 2: Analysis of Statement I
Since mutual internal forces between particles act along the lines joining them, the sum of internal torques about any origin cancels out completely (\(\boldsymbol{\tau}_{int} = \mathbf{0}\)). Consequently, the time rate of change of total angular momentum depends purely on the net external torque calculated about the same point. Therefore, Statement I is scientifically correct.

Step 3: Analysis of Statement II
Projecting the relation \(\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{L}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \boldsymbol{\tau}_{ext}\) along a specific axis (for example, the \(z\)-axis) yields \(\frac{\mathrm{d}L_z}{\mathrm{d}t} = \tau_{ext, z}\). When the external torque about this axis is zero (\(\tau_{ext, z} = 0\)), it follows directly that \(\frac{\mathrm{d}L_z}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0\), indicating that the angular momentum component \(L_z\) remains constant in time. Therefore, Statement II is scientifically correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct and Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_STATEMENT_BASED_2_Q06 - Characteristics and dynamic effects of force couples

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A couple is defined as a pair of forces of equal magnitude acting in opposite directions along parallel, non-collinear lines of action.

Statement II: When a couple acts on an unconstrained rigid body, it produces translational acceleration of the centre of mass as well as rotational acceleration.

In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Definition of a Force Couple
A couple consists of two forces \(\mathbf{F}\) and \(-\mathbf{F}\) having equal magnitudes and opposite directions, separated by a non-zero perpendicular distance (different lines of action).

Step 2: Analysis of Statement I
Because the two forces have equal magnitudes, opposite directions, and act along distinct parallel lines of action, they fit the exact physical definition of a couple. Therefore, Statement I is scientifically correct.

Step 3: Analysis of Statement II
The net resultant force of a couple is \(\mathbf{F}_{net} = \mathbf{F} + (-\mathbf{F}) = \mathbf{0}\). According to Newton's second law for extended bodies, the translational acceleration of the centre of mass is \(\mathbf{a}_{cm} = \frac{\mathbf{F}_{net}}{M} = \mathbf{0}\). However, the torque produced by the couple is non-zero (\(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F} \neq \mathbf{0}\)), generating pure rotational acceleration without any translational motion. Therefore, Statement II is scientifically incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Statement I is correct and Statement II is incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct and Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_STATEMENT_BASED_2_Q07 - Coincidence of centre of mass and gravity

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The centre of gravity of an extended body coincides with its centre of mass regardless of whether the ambient gravitational field is uniform or non-uniform.

Statement II: The spatial location of the centre of mass of a rigid body shifts depending on variations in local gravitational acceleration.

In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Distinction Between Centre of Mass and Centre of Gravity
The centre of mass is a geometric property of a body determined solely by its mass distribution: \(\mathbf{R}_{cm} = \frac{1}{M}\int \mathbf{r}\,\mathrm{d}m\). In contrast, the centre of gravity is the point about which the net torque due to gravitational forces on all constituent mass elements is zero: \(\sum \mathbf{r}_i \times (m_i \mathbf{g}_i) = \mathbf{0}\).

Step 2: Analysis of Statement I
If the gravitational field \(\mathbf{g}\) is uniform over the body, \(\mathbf{g}\) can be factored out of the torque equation, yielding \((\sum m_i \mathbf{r}_i) \times \mathbf{g} = \mathbf{0}\), so the centre of gravity coincides with the centre of mass. In a non-uniform gravitational field (such as across very large astronomical bodies), different portions experience different gravitational acceleration values, causing the centre of gravity to deviate from the centre of mass. Therefore, Statement I is scientifically incorrect.

Step 3: Analysis of Statement II
The centre of mass depends strictly on the spatial distribution of mass within the body (\(\mathbf{R}_{cm} = \frac{\sum m_i \mathbf{r}_i}{\sum m_i}\)) and is entirely independent of any external gravitational field or gravitational acceleration. Therefore, Statement II is scientifically incorrect.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct and Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_SYSTEMS_OF_PARTICLES_AND_ROTATIONAL_MOTION_STATEMENT_BASED_2_Q08 - Alignment of angular momentum and rotation axis

questiontext.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For any arbitrary rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, the total angular momentum vector is always strictly parallel to the angular velocity vector.

Statement II: For a symmetric rigid body rotating about a principal axis of symmetry, the perpendicular components of angular momentum sum to zero across opposite mass elements.

In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Angular Momentum Formulation for a Rotating Body
For a rigid body rotating with angular velocity \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\) about a fixed axis, the angular momentum of an individual mass element \(m_i\) at position \(\mathbf{r}_i\) is \(\mathbf{L}_i = m_i (\mathbf{r}_i \times \mathbf{v}_i) = m_i [\mathbf{r}_i \times (\boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{r}_i)]\). In general, \(\mathbf{L}_i\) has a component parallel to the rotation axis as well as a component perpendicular to the rotation axis.

Step 2: Analysis of Statement I
For an asymmetric body rotating about an arbitrary fixed axis, the sum of the perpendicular components \(\sum \mathbf{L}_{i\perp}\) does not vanish. Consequently, the total angular momentum vector \(\mathbf{L}\) is tilted relative to \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\) and is not parallel to the rotation axis. Therefore, Statement I is scientifically incorrect.

Step 3: Analysis of Statement II
When a body possesses geometric reflection symmetry about the rotation axis, for every mass element \(m_i\) located at position \(\mathbf{r}_i\), there exists an identical mass element located diametrically opposite across the axis. The components of angular momentum perpendicular to the axis generated by these opposite pairs are equal in magnitude and directed opposite to each other, exactly cancelling out upon summation. Hence, the net angular momentum aligns strictly along the axis of rotation. Therefore, Statement II is scientifically correct.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct.

answer.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct and Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct.
